name: East Turkestan
scope: East Turkestan as a political project: the demand that the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria (Xinjiang) be an independent state named East Turkestan/Turkistan, run by and for its Turkic Muslim peoples rather than by China. Drawn from the scholarship on the 1933-34 Turkic-Islamic Republic of Eastern Turkestan (Lee), on the Khotan Emirate and the 1944-49 republic, the exile movement of Bughra and Alptekin, and the 1960s Eastern Turkistan People's Revolutionary Party (Evans), plus the 1999 East Turkestan National Congress and its successors in exile (Jamestown, RFA). Bughra's 1940 history is its own text. It excludes the Chinese official view of Xinjiang, and the militant Turkistan Islamic Party as the typical case; the broader Uyghur identity movement is the separate Uyghur nationalism entry, and the Chinese-language label 'East Turkestan forces' is not used as a definition.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Evans, ch. 2: 'East Turkestan belongs to the real masters of the territory, the Uighurs, the Taranchis, the Kazaks, the Kirghiz...', a native land 'inherited from our fathers'. The sources do not use the word indigenous, hence low.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Lee, ch. 1 and ch. 2: Sabit Damulla and the Khotan Emirs wanted an Islamic state governed by the Shariah independent of China, and Amin Bughra wanted the Shariah to be the only law of the oases. Niaz, the president, was more compromising, and Evans notes ideological diversity in both republics, so +1 not +2.

more-religion-public.rationale: Lee, ch. 1: the 1933 state styled itself the Turkic-Islamic Republic of Eastern Turkestan, and its founders (Sabit, the Emirs) wanted an Islamic state; Sufi leaders such as Bughra gave it its political structure (ch. 2). Niaz's compromises and the Soviet-backed second republic's secular line keep it at +1.

national-self-determination.rationale: Lee, ch. 1: Khoja Niaz's declaration of the 1933 republic told Nanjing that the people of Eastern Turkestan were exercising their right to self-determination. Evans, ch. 2 quotes the second republic's call that East Turkestan belongs to its own peoples. The claim is made for Eastern Turkestan's peoples, not stated as a universal rule, so +1.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Evans, ch. 2 quotes second-republic literature: 'There is no place in East Turkestan for Chinese colonial government or Chinese colonists'; Lee, ch. 1 gives Niaz's principle that those who do not belong in Xinjiang should go back where they came from. Both oppose Han settlement in the region.

separate-church-state.rationale: Lee, ch. 1 and 2: the leaders of the 1933 republic, Sabit Damulla and Amin Bughra, wanted an Islamic state under the Shariah as the only law, which contradicts strict separation. Niaz and the Soviet-backed second republic leaned the other way, so -1.

summary: East Turkestan names the demand for an independent state in the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria (Xinjiang) for its Turkic Muslim peoples, rejecting Chinese rule and the Chinese name Xinjiang. The 1933 republic fused Pan-Islamism and Pan-Turkism and aimed at an Islamic state under the Shariah; the 1944 republic was Soviet-backed; exile leaders (Bughra, Alptekin) kept the independence cause alive; and a 1960s Marxist-Leninist party sought a revolutionary break. Its sources record positions mainly on independence, Islam in public life and opposition to Han settlement; most other topics are undocumented.
